title: Polygamous sect leader gets 24 years in prison for child abuse after girls found in trailer
description: A polygamous sect leader already serving a 50-year federal sentence for orchestrating sex involving children was given another 24 years in prison Tuesday on separate state convictions for child abuse ...
fullText:
PHOENIX (AP) — A polygamous sect leader already serving a 50-year federal sentence for orchestrating sex involving children was given another 24 years in prison Tuesday on separate state convictions for child abuse for hauling girls in an unventilated trailer in Arizona.

Samuel Bateman, 50, was convicted of three child abuse counts stemming from an August 2022 traffic stop in Flagstaff that led to the discovery of three girls, ages 11 to 14, in the trailer. It had a makeshift toilet, sofa and camping chairs and lacked air conditioning and seat belts. Someone tipped off authorities about the trailer after seeing small fingers reaching through gaps in the doors.

Bateman, whose small group was an offshoot of the polygamous sect once led by Warren Jeffs, is currently serving 50 years in federal prison for coercing girls as young as 9 to submit to sex acts with him and other adults and for scheming to kidnap girls from protective custody.

Citing an "insane danger" to the girls in the trailer, among other factors, Judge Joshua Steinlage ordered Bateman to serve the state sentence after completing the 50-year federal sentence.

"I love these dear people with all my heart, and I had no intention in the entire world to harm them," said Bateman, who represented himself in the case and didn't make a plea for leniency during his sentencing hearing.

Victims urged the judge to reject Bateman's claims that he didn't mean to harm anyone.

One victim who was in the trailer when Bateman was pulled over described the psychological pain she suffered. The victim, who was then 14, said Bateman took advantage of her sexually when she was 12. She said she has had to undergo therapy to recover from "things that should have never happened to me as a child."

"He stole my childhood," she said.

The Associated Press does not typically name alleged victims of sexual assault.

Bateman, a self-proclaimed prophet, previously claimed to have more than 20 "spiritual wives," including 10 girls under the age of 18.

In the state case, Bateman acknowledged he knew the girls were in a hot trailer for hours and that the ventilation wasn't good, but he downplayed the conditions.

Bateman had claimed he thought the girls had gotten out when they stopped. He said he was as "shocked as could possibly be" when he learned that they were still inside when he was pulled over.

"Today's sentence is about accountability for the harm done to these young victims," Coconino County Attorney Ammon Barker said in a statement. "It also ensures that Mr. Bateman will never again be in a position to harm a child."

Federal authorities said Bateman traveled extensively between Arizona, Utah, Colorado and Nebraska as he built an offshoot network of the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, which historically has been based in the neighboring communities of Colorado City, Arizona, and Hildale, Utah.

He and his followers practiced polygamy, a legacy of the early teachings of the mainstream Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, which abandoned the practice in 1890 and now strictly prohibits it.

Bateman was one of the trusted followers of Jeffs, who previously led the sect and is serving a life sentence in Texas for sexual assault of children.

The influence of the polygamous sect has waned significantly over time in the towns where the sect has historically been based. In 2017, a court order placed the towns under supervision, excising the church from their governments and shared police department.

The area has since transformed so quickly that the towns were released from court-ordered supervision last summer, almost two years earlier than expected. Practicing sect members are now believed to account for only a small percentage of the towns' populations.

Bateman was the focus of the Netflix series "Trust Me: The False Prophet."

title: Trump doesn’t seem to care what people want anymore
description: When President Donald Trump took the political world by storm in 2016, his rise was often described as a “populist” one. He seems to have abandoned that brand.
fullText:
When President Donald Trump took the political world by storm in 2016, his rise was often described as a "populist" one. And he certainly played the part of a renegade challenging a broken political system on behalf of regular Americans.

Ten years later, though, Trump has almost completely abandoned this brand of politics.

Indeed, in many ways, he has become the anti-populist.

And he's got the poll numbers to prove it.

Polling this month from Reuters and Ipsos has shown Trump's approval rating dropping to a record low of 33%. That's just 1 in 3 Americans who endorse his job performance.

But perhaps more telling is the still-falling percentage who "strongly" approve of him. It's been dropping for a while now. And in the newest poll, it's at just 13% of all Americans and 35% of Republicans.

That's roughly 1 in 8 Americans who think what Trump is doing is great — a remarkably small number of truly devoted supporters. And despite the president's supposed hammerlock on his base, nearly two-thirds of Republicans are less than enthused.

So how does a president get to that point?

For Trump, it's by almost totally disregarding public opinion in favor of his own whims, desires and even personal enrichment and glorification — a propensity he seems inclined to continue even during the stretch run of the midterms, when many politicians are highly sensitive to what plays well with voters.

Trump's threatened 50% tariffs on Canada are a case in point.

A CNN poll this spring showed 65% of Americans said Trump's tariffs had a negative impact on their personal finances. And even when the tariffs as a whole weren't as unpopular last year, his initial Canada levies were still very unpopular; between 60% and 64% of Americans opposed them from the outset.

So what does Trump do 70 days before the midterms? Embrace a trade war with Canada, naturally.

Trump on Tuesday even threatened to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America as part of the feud — echoing his purported renaming of the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America. Around two-thirds of Americans also opposed the latter change.

Vice President JD Vance got in on the act Monday by mislabeling Canada as a "state" and calling it a "Freudian slip" — evoking Trump's threats to make Canada the 51st state. And why not? A Marquette University Law School poll last year, after all, showed 75% of Americans opposed this idea.

Trump's recent positive comments about data centers are also perplexing for a supposed populist.

There is perhaps no more clear-cut populist issue right now than opposing data centers. As many as 7 in 10 Americans oppose having them in their communities, largely perceiving the centers as something powerful tech companies are inflicting upon them.

But even as his fellow Republicans turn sharply against them, Trump is embracing them. He's calling data centers "big, strong, bold, and Money Machines" and "Cash Cows." He said communities should welcome them and praised their architecture as the "most incredible buildings I've ever seen." He's even criticized Republicans for supporting moratoriums that ban data center development.

But these are hardly the only examples of Trump's anti-populism:

Polls show 6 in 10 Americans say Trump has "gone too far" in changing institutions like the Kennedy Center, and just 9% of Americans think it's appropriate to name government buildings after Trump while he's still president. Yet Trump is again trying to slap his name on the Kennedy Center.

He continues to focus extensively on his renovations of DC — often parading them for the cameras like he did with the new White House helipad Monday. This despite a Washington Post poll last month showing Americans viewed these kinds of projects negatively by a 2-to-1 margin.

The Iran war was clearly not what Americans wanted from the start; they opposed intervention by 2-to-1 margins in prewar polls. And Trump's supposed anti-war streak was core to his populism. Yet six months after launching the war, Trump is now threatening to extend the conflict through the midterms.

He's continued his factually deprived assault on vaccines this month, even as KFF polling shows 6 in 10 Americans oppose the administration's handling of the issue.

Trump until a few weeks ago seemingly wouldn't let go of his $1.776 billion "anti-weaponization" fund, which the White House has said could send money to violent January 6, 2021, defendants. This despite a poll last year showing 83% of Americans opposed Trump decision to pardon those people — much less paying them.

The problem with most of those examples isn't just that Trump is focused on his unpopular pet projects. It's that he's focused on them to the exclusion of and often at the expense of what people really want, which is a laser focus on affordability and economic issues.

He instead repeatedly talks about how we're in an economic "golden age," even though just 4% of Americans in the new Reuters-Ipsos poll said the economy was "very strong."

And people have noticed, with polls showing overwhelming majorities believe that he's neglecting the most important issues like inflation.

It all begs the question: What do voters do when a president basically casts off even the veneer of interest in doing what the people want — and instead does a series of things he wants that even large segments of his base appear uncomfortable with?

It sets up a pretty remarkable test of partisanship in the 2026 midterms.

title: Lutnick’s last-minute demands derailed Canada trade talks: Reports
description: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s interventions in the U.S.-Canada trade talks helped the weeks-long negotiations fall apart, according to multiple reports, thrusting the two countries into a trade ...
fullText:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's interventions in the U.S.-Canada trade talks helped the weeks-long negotiations fall apart, according to multiple reports, thrusting the two countries into a trade war.

U.S. and Canadian officials had felt good about an outline of a trade deal struck last Tuesday ahead of the original Wednesday deadline. President Trump took to social media to say that a deal had been struck, and he was pausing the 50 percent tariffs on some Canadian goods until Friday to finalize the paperwork.

But Lutnick was leery of Canadian proposals that would lower the tariff on autos to a level lower than what he wanted, according to The New York Times. He said instead that only a certain volume of aluminum should get lower tariff rates, and that heavy trucks should not have tariffs lowered like cars.

Canada produces some heavy trucks at the General Motors and Ford plants in Ontario.

Canadians put the blame on Lutnick for moving the goalposts at the eleventh hour, according to Bloomberg, while some business leaders were happy he was making demands on a deal they saw as hurting the U.S. metals industries.

When asked Saturday whether Lutnick's involvement in the final days of negotiations was an impediment, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that's "a question for the U.S. administration."

Carney said his Canadian team was "unified … but you cannot say that about the United States administration."

The talks between the U.S. and Canada fell apart on Friday, just hours before the tariffs were set to go into effect on items including wine, hockey sticks, cement and others.

Canada vowed to "match those tariffs dollar for dollar." The tariffs apply to around $20 billion of Canadian goods.

Since then, Trump has threatened further hits on Canada — in the form of 50 percent tariffs on cars, trucks, auto parts and steel that would go into effect on New Year's Day.

He accused Canada of "ripping off the United States of America for years" in a Truth Social post.

"On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with," he wrote. "They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON'T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US! They do 95% of their business with the U.S., with us, the exact opposite!"

Canada said Monday it is expected to unveil retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. on Tuesday. They would go into effect on Sept. 8.

title: The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Is 'Gucci Morty'?
description: Catch up on this week's viral trends with our guide to the Gucci Morty meme, Chanty Beluga, and more.
fullText:
This week's crop of things-that-only-matter-to-young people includes Gucci Morty and Chanty Beluga, two unrelated but incredibly popular meme characters, stolen source code for the biggest video game in the world, and a viral YouTube video that cost more than your house. So get ready to learn what's what and who's who among the younger generations.

Denizens of the internet create countless hundreds of thousands of memes every day, but only a tiny percentage ever gain any traction, and only one in a million really takes off. Gucci Morty is that meme this week. The image is of Morty from Rick and Morty wearing a black Gucci shirt and looking nonchalant ... and that's it. That's the whole thing.

I wouldn't have looked twice, but millions of younger people connected with the meme. Since he showed up about a week ago, Gucci Morty spread as fast as smallpox, from Instagram to TikTok to X to everywhere young people spread memes. Variations and tributes appeared, accompanied by part of "Lot of Me" by the rapper Lil Tecca, the song that gave Gucci Morty his catch phrase, "I can see you wanna vibe with me." Here's an example:

People started dressing as Gucci Morty:

It became a whole thing, with anyone under a certain age knowing Gucci Morty. But what does it mean? Why this meme? It's mostly ironic, with commenters noting Gucci Morty's endless aura, and memers putting him in "cool" situations. But the viral spread of Gucci Morty has become part of the joke, which has created a meme feedback loop, where people are posting Gucci Morty because there are so many memes of him, or posting videos where they comment on his all-of-a-sudden-everywhere nature:

Commenters seem to agree that Gucci Morty will vanish as quickly as he appeared, so get your fill now, before he becomes a "remember that one meme ..." in a few weeks.

Gucci Morty isn't the only inexplicable viral star this week. There's also Chanty Beluga. A character created by comedian Courtney O'Donnell, Chanty Beluga is a friendly woman who likes to say "Hi, I'm Chanty Beluga" while she's doing things like ordering food, getting a coffee, or making a doctor's appointment. The videos are generally about five seconds long and get millions of views. Her popularity seems to come from a couple sources: 1) "Chanty Beluga" is a funny name. 2) The brief interactions include suggestions of a larger, stranger life for Chanty, which is never explored. Chanty Beluga buys a portable cryo-chamber on Facebook Marketplace. She's served with legal papers. She's "reading for the part of Crypt Keeper." It's not much to account for all the views, but some things just hit for people and you gotta shrug.

There is no more eagerly awaited video game than Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto VI. Scheduled for release on November 19, 2026, Grand Theft Auto VI is is a game just about every gamer wants to play—but a few people are actually doing it. Mysterious hacker group Cyberleek has somehow gotten hold of a playable build of the game and has uploaded at least 10 gameplay videos to a Telegram Channel and a website. From there, they quickly spread everywhere, giving everyone an illicit peak of what to expect when this hits the market. But this is no viral marketing gimmick. Rockstar Games and its parent company Take-Two Interactive are furiously issuing subpoenas to Discord, Microsoft, and hosting providers to pull IP addresses and accounts linked to Cyberleek, nuking the videos when they appear. Right now, Cyberleek's site and Telegram are down, but I wouldn't be surprised if that does not stop them from posting more videos in the coming day. Cyberleek's drops are often couched in a message decrying digital-only game releases, but the real motivation isn't altruism, it's a crypto-currency scheme. Cyberleek has published a poll on its website where people can vote on what to show next through purchasing "CyberLeek" memecoin. As yet, there's no information on how, exactly, this group got its hands on GTA VI source code, leading to theories that a disgruntled employee made off with the code, or that some kind of phishing or other attack was wildly successful. The leaks are not expected to delay or alter "Grand Theft Auto 6: An Extended Look," a special streaming on Netflix beginning on August 27, nor should it affect the release date.

"Misery girl" is slang for a young women with piercings, a penchant for the darkly dramatic, and highly stylized makeup that makes them appear to have a skinny, pointy nose and huge eyes and lips. Here's the kind of look a Misery Girl sports:

And here's a makeup tutorial if you want to try the look yourself:

The Misery Girl gets her name from the fact that she supposedly likes the song "Misery" by Pupsies, which you can listen to below (if you dare).

Memes about Misery Girls frequently include the phrase "Dada, play that Misery," a reference to ageplay, which misery girls are supposed to be into. They often include pictures of X user @himonkeyhamie, who I'm sure deserves none of this. Misery Girl is not a self-selected nomenclature like "goth" or "emo," and there don't seem to be a ton of people rocking the look or lifestyle. Ultimately, it's a term used almost exclusively as a slur; as many have pointed out, it's all basically an excuse weirdos use to bully altgirls.

Back in 2017, unknown YouTuber Jimmy "MrBeast" Donaldson went viral for the first time by sitting in his room counting 100,000. That no-budget webcam stunt was enough to get millions of views on YouTube back then. This week's viral video from MrBeast has nearly 45 million views after only three days online, and it proves that you really have to up the production if you expect to go viral with a stunt video in 2026. Escape 100 Cops, Win $500,000 is among the most elaborate video ever shot for YouTube. MrBeast hired 100 off-duty Indiana State Police troopers to try to catch him and four of his friends as they hid out in a simulated town rigged with tunnels, explosives, secret rooms and more. Anyone who avoids capture for 12 hours gets a $100,000. The police department gets $500,000 if everyone is apprehended. The video required a huge production crew, legal department for the permits, explosive experts, post production department, and more. Judging from what MrBeast has said in the past about his more elaborate videos, the budget was comfortably in the multimillion dollar range.

title: 10 Shows Like 'Modern Family' You Should Watch Next
description: Modern families for every mood.
fullText:
The family sitcom, once a staple, has become a bit more rare over the past decade or so—but when one hits, as Modern Family did over the course of its eleven seasons, it hits big. Gone but not forgotten, the show continues to remind us that, hey—families DO come in all shapes and sizes, and that's not just fine—it's great actually. In that spirit, here are some other shows that invite us into the lives of big ol' families living the American and/or Canadian dream.

Like Modern Family, Life in Pieces follows a large extended family (in California, no less) through trials both relatable and zany. Joan (Dianne Wiest) and John (James Brolin) head a family that includes Colin Hanks, Betsy Brandt, and Thomas Sadoski, with the clever conceit that each episode includes four distinct stories looking in on different members of the family; the stories often (but don't always) dovetail, but the format allows us to follow a huge cast of characters without a need for people to constantly be showing up at each other's houses. Clever. Stream Life in Pieces on Hulu.

One of our most recent great family sitcoms, focuses on a slightly smaller ensemble than that of Modern Family while still dealing with the challenges of a large intergenerational family—it also follows a similar format in that dad Dre (Anthony Anderson) narrates episodes in not-quite mockumentary style. Anderson is joined by Tracee Ellis Ross, playing a pair of successful Black parents at the head of a family dealing with typical stuff while also trying to reconcile staying true to cultural identities while living in the rich white suburbs. Kids Yara Shahidi and Marcus Scribner later split the spin-off Mixed-ish, while Dre's outspoken mother Ruby (the brilliant Jenifer Lewis) steals every scene. Stream Black-ish on Hulu and Netflix.

This comedy, inspired by Norman Lear’s beloved 1975 sitcom of the same name, quickly became one of the streamer’s most critically acclaimed shows, telling the story of a Latinx family lead by Justina Machado as Lupe Alvarez, an Army Nurse Corps veteran struggling with her return to civilian life and single motherhood (she’s joined by the scene-stealing Rita Moreno as her delightfully plainspoken mother). Aside from that solid Latinx representation, the funny and big-hearted show spotlighted Justina’s lesbian daughter, Elena, and her non-binary love interest, Syd—making for a wonderfully and appropriately modern family. Stream One Day at a Time on Netflix.

Quickly establishing itself as one of the great workplace mockumentaries, and ABC's immediate successor to Modern Family in ratings success, Quinta Brunson's Abbott Elementary portrays its cast of (mostly) well-meaning characters running up against an American educational system that doesn't always reward good intentions. Set at work rather than home, the themes are different but the tone is similar, with the staff at Abbott functioning as a goofy tight-knit family, sharing their dreams, frustrations, and sassy commentary with the camera. The 2022 Emmy win for the great Sheryl Lee Ralph became a viral moment, if only because it was so well-deserved for an actress representing an incredibly talented, brilliantly funny cast. Stream Abbott Elementary on Hulu and HBO Max.

A bit of a spiritual successor to Roseanne as one of our great working-class sitcoms, Malcolm in the Middle represented the economic reality that had firmly taken hold in the real world—the fact that an office job, once seen as a big a step up, is no longer a symbol of prosperity. It's also a show about how a thoroughly zany and dysfunctional family can love with the same excess that they approach everything else with. The recent follow-up miniseries, Life's Still Unfair, is the rare revival that hits the mark. Stream Malcolm in the Middle on Hulu.

The Kims are a Korean-Canadian family running the title convenience store in Toronto, with Paul Sun-Hyung Lee and Jean Yoon leading the cast as the traditionally minded parents, along with a pre-Marvel Simu Liu as son Jung and Andrea Bang as daughter Janet. The show walks a deft line, bitingly dealing with issues facing immigrant families, in particular, but rarely if ever never at the expense of the comedy—mining plenty of laughs from the generation gap between Umma and Appa and the kids. Stream Kim's Convenience on Peacock.

Though never exactly buzzy, The Middle ran for an impressive (and remarkably consistent) nine seasons without relying on any particular storytelling gimmick or high concept: just the story of the Heck family, living in the fictional Orson, Indiana. Frankie (Patricia Heaton) begins the show as a salesperson at a used-car dealership before becoming a dental assistant, while husband Mike (Neil Flynn) manages a quarry. The show blends a bit of Malcolm in the Middle-style portrait of a sometimes chaotic family (barely) balancing work and kids with Modern Family's more sentimental leanings. Stream The Middle on Peacock and Prime Video.

Lauren Graham (Gilmore Girls) plays single mother Sarah, at the head of a large ensemble cast playing members of the extended Braverman family in Berkeley, California. Not a comedy, but not (usually) a heavy-heavy drama, either, involving typical family trials across six seasons. Craig T. Nelson plays the family patriarch with Graham, Peter Krause, Dax Shepard, and Erika Christensen as the four kids, each with families of their own—providing story opportunities that the show mines ably. Stream Parenthood on Paramount+.

Where Parenthood is more of a comedy-drama, this is very much a drama-drama, and legendarily one of the most tear-jerking shows of the last decade or so—do not, I beg you, go into this expecting a lot of chuckles. Dan Fogelman's primetime drama was one of the buzziest shows of the late aughts, following the lives of the Pearson family over several decades. Introducing us to siblings Randall, Kate, and Kevin (Sterling K. Brown, Chrissy Metz, and Justin Hartley) in the present, episodes then takes us back to their early lives and those of their parents, Jack (Milo Ventimiglia) and Rebecca (Mandy Moore). Though it's not a match in tone, it's thematically surprisingly similar to Modern Family in that it's a big-hearted family show at its core, with lots of hugging and crying, and one that follows a large intergenerational family through good times and bad. Stream This is Us on Hulu and Tubi.

With a cast this impressive—the late, great Catherine O'Hara; Eugene and Daniel Levy; Annie Murphy; Emily Hampshire; etc. etc.—the story here could be entirely incidental but, of course, this who's who of Canadian comedy talent is given plenty to work with. Having been defrauded by a business manager, the once-wealthy Rose family is forced to relocate to the title town and trying to rebuild their lives, living and working in a run-down hotel. Though the Rose family no longer has any reason for snobbery, old habits die hard, and there's comedy gold to be mined from their efforts to fit in. Stream Schitt's Creek on Hulu and HBO Max.

title: Five Hacks Every Amazfit T-Rex 3 Pro User Should Know
description: Finally, a watch that lets your dog track their workouts, too.
fullText:
Amazfit's T-Rex 3 Pro has a lot of great headline features: A titanium bezel, a sapphire display, multi-week battery life, and on-device route planning for its “pro” version. And at $399.99, it's still on the budget end compared to similarly feature-rich rugged sports watches. Turns out, you can get even more out of this watch with some Amazfit-specific hacks. Here are five features in the Amazfit T-Rex Pro that go a bit beyond the manual.

In the Zepp app, go to Profile > Settings > About, then tap the Zepp logo seven times. Voilà: You've just unlocked developer mode. It's a fun rabbit hole if you like poking around under the hood, and it can occasionally be useful for troubleshooting sync issues or checking firmware details that the standard interface hides from you.

Developer mode also lets you install custom watch faces, rather than relying on the existing native watch face library and upload a custom face on your computer, scan a generated QR code, and install it directly onto your watch.

Most users know their T-Rex 3 Pro has a built-in flashlight, activated with a long press of the UP button, and the Pro version specifically pairs a white LED with a red one. The red light is the real hidden gem: it preserves your night vision, which matters if you're checking a map at a campsite or trying not to wake someone up while moving around a dark room. The flashlight also doubles as an SOS strobe, so in an actual emergency you can trigger a flashing distress signal without fumbling for your phone. If you've only ever used the white beam, it's worth knowing that red mode and SOS strobe exist a tap away. After turning the flashlight on, here's how to use different modes:

Tap the flashlight icon on the screen, or quickly press the UP or DOWN buttons to cycle through normal white intensities and the low-interference red light mode.

Press the UP and DOWN buttons simultaneously to activate an ultra-bright beam. This mode lasts for up to 30 seconds and requires a brief cooldown period before you can use it again.

Pull down the watch screen to open the Control Center and tap SOS to start emergency signaling.

Go to Settings > Assistant (or Workout) > Safety Light to enable automatic flashing patterns while running or cycling in the dark.

The offline mapping system on the T-Rex 3 Pro goes further than your standard "record only" breadcrumb trail. Beyond simple point-to-point navigation, it supports round-trip routing, meaning you can tell the watch how far you want to go and it will generate a loop that brings you back to your starting point, no destination required. Pair that with auto-rerouting, which recalculates automatically if you wander off the planned path, and you get a level of route planning that used to be reserved for far pricier GPS watches. It's a great way to explore an unfamiliar trail network without any real risk of getting stuck trying to retrace your steps.

Here's how to use Amazfit's automatic round-trip route planning:

Open the map, wait for positioning, press SEL > Navigation > Create Round-Trip Route.

Choose workout type, direction, and target distance. The watch will generate a round-trip route automatically.

Tap Start Workout to begin, or Save Route to use later under My Route.

If you deviate more than 500 meters from the route during the workout, the watch will automatically trigger the route recalculation function.

Scroll past Running and Walking, select More Workouts, and you'll find Dog Walking mode. This way, you can keep a real history of outings with your pet separate from your personal training log. Because it's tucked a couple of menu levels deep, most owners never stumble across it and end up logging dog walks as generic walking sessions instead, losing that dedicated record.

If you have a T-Rex 3 Pro, you're probably who values getting out into nature, far away from screens and nonstop notifications. Still, you might want important alerts from your watch if you're heading out on a hike alone.

Head into your watch's settings and toggle individual watch app alerts on or off separately, so critical alarms and low-battery warnings still function even when everything else is muted. For app-specific control, the path is Notifications and Reminders, then App Notifications, then App Alerts, where you can enable only the handful of apps you actually care about, such as messages from a specific person, while keeping the rest of your wrist quiet during an outing. It's a small setup investment that pays off every time you're biking through the trails and don't want your wrist buzzing over a promotional email.

I'd like to leave you with a bonus hack, since I assume you're not afraid of inclement weather: Amazfit has a built-in water ejection feature. Water can linger in your watch's microphone and speaker ports, muffling sound or triggering false touches. Here's what to do: Swipe down from the main screen to open the Control Center, tap the Droplet icon, and hold your watch with the speaker facing downward. The watch will vibrate at specific frequencies designed to physically push moisture out of the ports. Like all the hacks above, this is one of those features it's good to know about now, so you're ready for the moment you really need it.

title: Is the Oura Ring Really Just Guessing at Your Sleep Score?
description: Spoiler: No sleep wearable was ever trustworthy in the first place.
fullText:
Oura is currently being sued over its claims that the ring measures your sleep. Both the law firm bringing the class action suit and Oura itself have released statements giving their opinion on the matter, and I’ll dig into those today. I also want to talk about the underlying issue here—how much can we trust our wearables when it comes to sleep data?

So, first, the lawsuit. It’s a class action suit being brought by Clarkson Law Firm out of California on behalf of Madison Surber, a person who bought an Oura ring. The suit states: “At the time of purchase, Plaintiff did not know that the Challenged Representations were false—i.e., that the Product could not accurately and definitively measure sleep stages.” You can read the full text here.

A press release from the law firm summarizes the problem like so: “The product cannot measure any of the physiological signals required to determine sleep quality or sleep stages. Instead, it delivers only AI-generated guesses that, according to the Complaint, are no more reliable than a coin flip.”

After the suit was filed, Oura published a blog post called “Standing Behind Our Science,” which you can read here. Oura writes: “A recent baseless, opportunistic legal allegation seeks to discredit how consumer wearables—including Oura Ring—track and estimate sleep stages. We dispute these allegations and stand firmly behind our research and accuracy.”

Beyond the suit being filed and both sides stating their position, nothing has officially happened yet, and it may be a while before we hear anything else. The case has not gone to trial, there has been no judgment, and Oura rings are still on the shelves for the foreseeable future.

It’s also worth remembering that plenty of lawsuits never even make it to trial; the two sides often end up coming to an agreement privately, and we may or may not hear what the terms of that settlement even are. It sometimes happens that a lawsuit is announced with sensational claims even if the suing party does not expect to win in the end. I’m no legal scholar, and I’m not qualified to judge who is likely to win this case or why it was brought. What I can talk about, though, is whether it’s reasonable to expect wearables to properly track our sleep.

As I write about fitness tech, I keep coming up against a fundamental problem: Companies make their devices report numbers, and device users want to know if those numbers are “accurate.” I do my best to judge the answer to that question, but it’s often impossible to answer.

Here’s why. First of all, only a measurement can be accurate: something like “how many beats per minute is my heartbeat?” (which I am actually able to test when I write about devices, as you may have noticed). If this measurement matches a gold-standard reference (ideally on multiple tests over time and with different people), we can judge how accurate it seems to be.

But most things a wearable reports are not, strictly speaking, measurements. They may be calculated from other data. The amount of time you were asleep is calculated from start and end times, and an algorithm had to “decide” when those start and end events happened. Similarly, even for something simple like counting steps, the device has to “know” what movement of the device should count as a step. That’s why we can get different step counts from different devices. And since a watch only has access to movement data from your wrist, it doesn’t know what your feet are doing. Indoor running mileage is also an estimate for those same reasons.

One step further removed from those stats are scores and interpretations. Some are obviously made up: A “79” sleep score doesn’t correspond to anything a scientist could measure in a lab. But sleep stages are also in this category. When Oura tells me I had 51 minutes of REM sleep last night, it doesn’t know this; it’s just putting together the data it has and making its best estimation. I’ve often told you guys not to read too much into sleep stages, but instead to take note of how long you’re sleeping in total, and to pay attention to real-world things like whether you feel tired during the day. My colleague Meredith Dietz came to a similar conclusion after interviewing sleep scientists for this look into why sleep scores are a lot less useful than you would think.

Let’s take this back to the basics. What is happening on the ring itself? An Oura ring can shine red and green (and infrared) LEDs on your skin, and its sensors pick up reflections of that light to get a decently good sense of your heart rate and an estimate of your blood oxygen. The ring has motion sensors, so it can tell when you (or at least your finger) are moving around. There is also a temperature sensor for skin temperature.

That’s it, as far as measurements in a strict sense. From the fluctuations in the rhythm of your heartbeat, Oura can calculate your respiration rate and HRV. From accelerometer data, it can calculate the times it thinks you are lying perfectly still. Oura has written here about what it measures and what it calculates or infers from those measurements. That blog post is about the Oura Ring 4 (which is also the device named in the lawsuit), but you can expect most smart rings and other wearables to work similarly.

So, the lawsuit is technically correct in saying that Oura doesn’t actually know your sleep stages. But Oura may be able to successfully argue that it’s as correct as you can expect a wearable to be.

I found one of the lawsuit’s claims interesting: “Plaintiff does not personally know the mechanism or science behind the Products’ promised sleep tracking features. ... Plaintiff had and still has no way of determining whether the Challenged Representations on the Products were and are true.”

Companies that make wearables don’t share their algorithms publicly. (Maybe there’s an exception to this rule, but I can’t think of any.) Both the device itself, and the software that interprets its readings aren’t subject to any thorough, public accuracy or validity testing before a device makes it to market.

That’s why tech writers like me have to make do with “N=1” tests: I, as one person, go for a few runs and report the data I got. I, as one person, sleep a few nights comparing the readings from multiple devices. I can’t rent a sleep lab for every device review, and if I could, I’d ideally bring a few hundred friends and a lot of research funding for a team of scientists to pore over the results. That’s just not in the Lifehacker budget. Ironically, tech reporters like me are the first—and in some cases, the only—people to do in-depth independent testing on wearable devices.

Sometimes scientists do proper studies, especially on devices that are popular or that might have uses in the clinic or for research. I’m glad for these studies, but they just don’t happen on a schedule that makes them useful to regular folks who want to know if a new device does what it says it does. By the time a paper comes out telling us how the Garmin Fenix 6 did at measuring heart rate during sleep, Garmin is already selling the Fenix 8. By the time you hear about it—perhaps today?—we're already on to the Fenix 9.

In a press release from the law firm, several of the lawyers stressed that customers make choices in their daily lives based on information they get from their wearables. This is true of all wearables, not just Oura, and I think it’s a fair point. We probably rely too much on data that we shouldn’t actually trust.

Something that doesn’t ring true to me is the claim from the lawsuit that “sleep happens in the brain, not on one’s finger. It is defined by brain electrical activity, eye movements, muscle tone, and other signals...” That quote almost had me in the first half, but sleep isn’t defined by EEG readings and such. It’s measured that way in the lab.

A scientist doing a sleep study is trying to eavesdrop on what your body is doing, and toward that end, scientists have described stages of sleep based on those signals. But sleep itself is still something of a mystery to science. Professional-grade equipment probably has a better handle on what’s going on than a consumer-grade ring, but both are just describing outward signs of an inscrutable internal process.

Oura points out in their “Standing Behind Our Science” blog that several scientific and medical teams have published peer-reviewed papers on Oura’s sleep data. I commend Oura for encouraging teams to study its devices. That said, lots of familiar problems crop up when you start looking at the studies.

The most recent, for example, is this 2024 study that compares the Gen 3 Oura ring (two models back) to the Fitbit Sense 2 and the Apple Watch Series 8—all pretty out-of-date models at this point. One of the authors is a consultant for Oura and serves on its Medical Advisory board. And I don’t find the results particularly impressive; it reports a sensitivity of 75% or better on detecting sleep stages, which may be slightly better than the other devices, but still supports my longstanding opinion that we should not put too much stock in any wearable’s claims about the stages or “quality” of your sleep.

And that's where I find myself after reading both sides' claims: A smart ring (or watch) is a tool that can report its measurements, estimations, and inferences. Some of these may be useful. But none of them are ever guaranteed to be accurate. Perhaps we should all forget about chasing accuracy and pay more attention to old-fashioned things like making sure you have a good bedtime routine.

title: Six Quintessential Movies to Watch in Honor of Dolly Parton
description: There will be a lot of tears, and a lot of life to celebrate.
fullText:
There are so few people on whom we can all agree, and that list has gotten smaller with the passing of Dolly Parton. While she'd suggested health struggles for some time, the death of Dolly always seemed impossible—or maybe just too cruel an outcome in a world with enough heartbreak already. But here we are, and even though there are going to be a lot of tears, there's a lot to celebrate.

It's her music, of course, that will live on, but her persona wasn't entirely built on songs. A larger-than-life personality with an outsized look (very much by design), her film presence is indelible, in spite of a relatively brief filmography. Her roles in two of the best films of the 1980s are so important to our cultural memories of that decade—and are so darn good—that it's hard to remember that she made that impact in just a handful of films (and a few more cameos) over the course of her career. Dolly may well have thrived in character parts and cameos, but she won and broke our hearts in movies like 9 to 5 and Steel Magnolias. It's easy to wish she'd acted more, but instead, we'll just be grateful for the absolute gems she left us.

The title song nearly overtakes the film in cultural currency, but the film itself opened the 1980s on a high note, ultimately promising a better decade than we actually got. The generational team-up of Dolly, Jane Fonda, and Lily Tomlin—three women with wildly different screen personas who played off of each other marvelously—grounds the uneven silliness of the movie with real heart and soul. The three office workers inadvertently poison their sexist, egotistical, lying, hypocritical bigot of a boss (a very game Dabney Coleman) and, in the process, bring down the office patriarchy and usher in a female-driven workers' paradise. Dolly as sexy secretary Doralee Rhodes is seen by the other women, initially, as a bimbo sleeping with the boss to get her way before they discover that she's just as smart, capable, and pissed off as they are, boobs and big hair notwithstanding. The related album is just as interesting, a rare case of Dolly tipping her political hand and offering up songs about workers' rights and immigration. This is where Dolly's film career began, and it's a doozy. Stream 9 to 5 on Prime Video.

This doesn't sound like a movie to win awards, and it didn't, but Dolly did pick up her second Golden Globe nomination for Best Actress. The movie, a musical with Dolly as the proprietor of a Texas brothel, finds her in a relationship with the local Sheriff (Burt Reynolds, who else?) while a local news personality (played by Dom DeLuise) plans an expose that will bring the Miss Mona's Chicken Ranch down. Dolly largely plays to type here, but it's all in good fun and not entirely devoid of substance: The hypocritical and puritanical reporter presages the increasingly loud and puritanical style of reporting that was soon to take over the news. Rent The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas from Prime Video.

Nearly a decade after 9 to 5, Dolly joined another all-time great ensemble of women, this time with Sally Field, Shirley MacLaine, Daryl Hannah, Olympia Dukakis, and Julia Roberts. Hannah's mousy Annelle Dupuy, new in town, introduces us to Chinquapin Parish in Louisiana, and the daily lives of some of its residents. Dolly plays hairdresser (sorry: glamour technician) Truvy Jones, and there's a rather brilliant contrast between her physical performance (this is very much the extravagantly big-haired Dolly we know and love) and her character, who's very much the calm center of the film's various storms. She's the exuberant town gossip, but she's also everyone's rock during hard times. Stream Steel Magnolias on Paramount+.

As a rom-com, Straight Talk is...perfectly fine, though the pairing of Dolly and James Woods is hardly one for the ages. But the movie shines when we're not dealing with any of that and are focusing on Dolly as a plain-spoken radio host who is, as one of the songs on the memorable soundtrack reminds us, Livin' a Lie. She's dance instructor Shirlee Kenyon, divorced and fired from her job for running her mouth when she ought to be teaching. On her first day at her new job as a receptionist, she wanders into the studio and is mistaken for the clinical doctor who's meant to be giving advice—which she winds up doing on an increasingly popular talk show, even though her credentials are entirely fake (Woods is the reporter trying to expose her who later becomes a love interest). Dolly offering up plainspoken advice is such an appealing proposition that it's hard to fault the movie even where it doesn't work. Rent Straight Talk from Prime Video.

Two women battle, and ultimately join together, to save a small-town church choir in Pacashau, Ga. Dolly plays G. G. Sparrow, widow of longtime choir director Bernard (Kris Kristofferson), who believes herself to be his natural successor—at least until she's pushed aside by Vi Rose Hill (Queen Latifah). But, when the choir is pushed out of the annual "Joyful Noise" competition, funding begins to dry up, and the two have to put aside their differences and blend their styles to save the day. The movie rides almost entirely on its music and the chemistry of its central pairing—but, when we're talking about Dolly Parton and Queen Latifah (alongside Keke Palmer and Jeremy Jordan), that's very nearly enough. Rent Joyful Noise from Prime Video.

Dolly has a key, if entirely supporting, role in this Christmas confection. It’s the holidays, and Regina Fuller (Christine Baranski) is on her way home to evict a bunch of people so she can sell the land they live on to a mall developer. Naturally, she’s got some seasonal learning to do, with help from erstwhile bestie Margeline (Jenifer Lewis) and Dolly herself, playing to type as an all-singing angel. Dolly wrote all the musical numbers, Debbie Allen did the choreography, and the results are pretty darn delightful, especially during the chilly holiday months. Stream Christmas on the Square.

title: 10 Hacks Every Apple Wallet User Should Know
description: Get the most out of your Wallet.
fullText:
For those in the Apple ecosystem, Apple Wallet is a powerful hub for making digital payments, storing tickets and passes, and transferring cash. There are also a handful of hidden features that ensure you have quick and easy access to your cards and can customize how they're used on your iPhone and Apple Watch. Here are the hacks you need to know to get the most out of Wallet.

Express Mode in Apple Wallet allows you to use transit cards (and payment cards specifically for transit), keys, student IDs, and other compatible passes without waking your device or authenticating with Face ID, Touch ID, or your passcode. These passes are also available on a battery reserve, so you can still use them even if your iPhone is dead. This means you can still get home on public transit or unlock your door without needing to charge your device first. Select the card, pass, or key in Apple Wallet, tap the three dots > Card Details > Express Transit Settings or Express Mode.

It's worth noting that Express Mode would allow anyone with physical access to your device to use your passes since authentication isn't required. You may want to keep keys secured with biometrics and reserve Express Mode for transit cards, which you're more likely to need to tap and go.

Apple Pay is increasingly accepted as a payment option online, in apps, and at brick-and-mortar merchants, but there are still plenty of places that won't accept a direct Apple Pay transaction. If you're shopping online or making a payment over the phone, you can generate a virtual card number for Apple Cash, which allows you to spend those funds directly and also keeps your real card information hidden. When you select your Apple Cash card in Wallet, tap the card icon at the top of the screen and authenticate to get the number. The three-digit security code will change each time you use AutoFill or access your card in Wallet.

If you use different payment cards for different transaction types—one card offers better rewards on groceries while another is good for gas, for example—Apple Wallet can automatically suggest the correct one based on your location so you don't have to remember which is which or manually select a card each time you check out. (This is also handy for pulling up digital loyalty cards or membership passes as soon as you walk in the door.) This relies on a custom automation through Shortcuts. In the Library tab, tap the "+" button, type "Card" into the search bar, and select Open Card. Then go to Automation, tap "+," select Arrive and add the Location. You can select when to run the automation, then hit Next. For the Action, select Open Card in Wallet, select the pass or card, and confirm.

Many methods of peer-to-peer payment require you to obtain some type of contact information—such as a username, email, or phone number—from the person you're sending money to or receiving money from. If they're your friend or you pay them often using a service like Venmo or Cash App, this probably isn't a hassle. But you could use Apple Wallet's built-in Tap to Cash, which transfers money instantly between two iPhones or Apple Watches without sharing private contact information. You simply need to have Apple Cash set up in advance. When you're ready to send or receive funds, open Wallet, tap your Apple Cash card, and select Send or Request > Tap to Cash. Enter the amount, tap Next, double-click your iPhone side button to confirm, and hold your device up to the other person's.

Apple Wallet can securely store a few different types of digital keys: home, apartment/condo, hotel room, car, and scooter. Your device will automatically pull up the correct key when you're in range of the lock, and you can also enable Express Mode so you don't need to authenticate with Face ID or your passcode. Car and scooter keys can then be shared, so other drivers can lock, unlock, and start your vehicle without needing a physical key. You can also set custom permissions, such as restricting the recipient's ability to reshare and, depending on the car manufacturer, setting limits on things like speed and radio volume.

When you select your car key in Wallet and tap Share, set the available permissions, add an optional activation code, and choose your recipient. You can share via Messages, Mail, WhatsApp, and AirDrop, to name a few.

In addition to showing you recent transactions on each of your cards, Wallet serves as a hub for tracking orders on purchases made with Apple Pay. You just have to enable this in Settings > Wallet & Apple Pay > Order Tracking. (Also in beta is an Apple Intelligence and Siri feature that can update orders in Wallet with information pulled from Mail—this is a separate toggle in Settings.) Back in Wallet, tap the three dots > Orders.

Apple has continued to expand its digital ID options within Wallet so you can add your driver's license and/or state ID as well as your passport to the app and use your iPhone—instead of the physical documents—to verify your identity. Practically speaking, this is most useful when flying, as digital IDs are accepted at TSA checkpoints. (It's worth noting that only a small subset of states have compatibility with Apple Wallet.) You may also be able to use your ID from Wallet at some entertainment venues, as well for in-app verifications. Tap the "+" sign in Wallet, select Driver's License and ID Cards, choose the ID you want to add, and follow the prompts.

While Apple Pay is relatively seamless for online purchases if you're using a Mac and Safari, there are other cases where you can't authenticate payment simply by using Touch ID—for example, you have your laptop docked and closed or you're using an older device without built-in biometrics. On a non-Safari browser, you also have to scan a generated code with your iPhone to complete an Apple Pay purchase. While you can't get around the latter, you can enable Allow Payments on Mac for the former, which then lets you authenticate from your iPhone or Apple Watch if it's not possible to do on desktop. Go to Settings > Wallet & Apple Pay > Allow Payments on Mac.

While many types of passes—library cards, event tickets, membership passes, etc.—already integrate seamlessly with Apple Wallet, some businesses may still hand out physical cards. If you want to digitize, you can use a third-party app like MakePass or Pass2U Wallet to scan and add unsupported cards to Apple Wallet. iOS 27 is coming out with a Create a Pass feature that will do this natively via Apple Intelligence.

If you use Apple Pay for recurring charges, such as subscriptions and monthly bills, you can view a list of merchants right in Wallet. Tap the three dots in the upper right corner and select Preauthorized Payments. You can also revoke payment tokens, though Apple notes that this won't cancel your subscription and associated payment—rather, it'll simply communicate to the merchant not to charge the Apple Pay method again. To actually cancel or change your payment method, you'll have to go directly to the merchant.

title: 10 Hacks Every iOS 27 User Should Know
description: These 10 hacks are essential for anyone upgrading to iOS 27.
fullText:
If you have an iPhone 11 or newer (including the second-gen iPhone SE), you can look forward to installing iOS 27 in the fall. Apple's next big update is heavy on the AI and stability upgrades, and will likely drop sometime in September. However, iOS 27 has also been available in beta all summer. I've been running the update on my primary iPhone for nearly three months now, and during that time, I've discovered a bunch of hacks I think every iOS 27 user should know. Whether you're installing the update today or next month, you should definitely try out these useful hacks for your iPhone.

Apple introduced Liquid Glass with iOS 26, and didn't hold back with its design choices. While some liked the changes, others have criticized Liquid Glass for focusing more on style over substance. In response, cApple introduced new ways to adjust and customize the design's transparency effects. That only continues with iOS 27. There's now a new slider that lets you reduce or almost eliminate the Liquid Glass effect. You can find it under Settings > Appearance > Liquid Glass in iOS 27. Move the slider towards the right to improve readability.

I've lost count of the number of times I've accidentally sent incomprehensible voice notes to people on iMessage. In my case, the culprit was the audio message button to the right of the text box in the Messages app. Luckily, in iOS 27, you can either change that button to dictation, or remove it altogether. To change it up, head over to Settings > Apps > Messages, and select Show in Text Field. You can pick one of these three choices: Record Audio, Start Dictation, and None. The last one (None) removes the audio message button from the text box. Note that you can still access the "Audio" option from the (+) menu, while dictation will appear in your keyboard.

With iOS 27, Apple is making it possible to set different volume levels for ringtones, alerts, and alarms. If you want to silence app notifications and texts, but still hear your ringtones and alarms, this one's for you. To set it up, go to Settings > Sounds & Haptics, and turn off Match Ringtone Volume under "Alarms and Timers." You can now use the slider to set a different volume level for those two features. Similarly, you can turn off Match Ringtone Volume under "Alerts and System Sounds," and move the slider according to your needs.

iOS 27 introduces a convenient new slider that lets you set timers from the Dynamic Island on your iPhone. To use it directly from the Lock Screen, however, you'll have to remove one of the two controls already present. Pick up your iPhone, and allow Face ID to unlock the device without leaving the Lock Screen. Now, tap and hold the screen, then tap Customize near the base of the display. Tap the "-" button next to the two controls near the bottom-right and bottom-left corners of the display. By default, these two controls are for the flashlight and camera, respectively. After deleting one control, press the + button that appears in its place, and select Timer from the list of controls. Tap the Done button in the top-right corner. Now, when you tap this button, you'll see a slider appear from the Dynamic Island up top. Move the slider to set a timer, and tap Start Timer to get it going.

With iOS 27, you can essentially start a livestream from FaceTime for the people you're calling. A new feature called "Dual Capture" allows you to record and stream video from both the front camera and the rear camera simultaneously. This means that you can show your face and the things around you during a FaceTime call, so you don't have to pick one or the other at any given moment.

To use this feature, start a FaceTime video call with another person, and tap the "Flip" button that appears in your selfie video frame. This will start a Dual Capture session. You can stop streaming both cameras by tapping the Flip button in the bottom-left corner of the screen, which returns you to a regular selfie video. In addition, you can turn off the front camera feed in a FaceTime call. When in Dual Capture mode, tap the button that appears in the top-left corner of your front camera feed, the icon with a crossed-out person. This turns off the front camera stream, and lets you show just the feed off the rear camera. Note that Dual Capture is limited to iPhone Air, iPhone 17 series, and newer devices.

If you or your gym has GymKit-compatible equipment, you can connect your Apple Watch to the machines to track your workouts. I use this feature all the time, but, of course, if I forget to wear my Apple Watch, or if it runs out of charge, then my workouts don't get logged. Apple is fixing this problem by bringing GymKit compatibility to iPhones. With iOS 27, you'll be able to connect your iPhone directly to compatible treadmills, elliptical machines, indoor bikes, and other cardio equipment. Whether you don't have an Apple Watch, or don't have access to it, you can continue tracking your workouts with greater levels of accuracy.

Setup is easy: As explained by 9to5Mac, you can tap your iPhone against a GymKit-enabled machine, like a treadmill, then follow the on-screen instructions to set up and track a workout, such as "Indoor Run" or "Indoor Walk." All data is removed from the machine at the end of the session, and stored directly on your iPhone. Note that this feature won't necessarily track your heart rate. However, if you have a pair of AirPods Pro 3, you can use the built-in heart rate sensor to track your workout.

If you're tired of typos when you're dictating something to your iPhone, use iOS 27's "Advanced Dictation Preview." The new feature uses Siri AI to upgrade dictation's accuracy, and polishes text automatically—similar to Google's Rambler feature. Apple says Siri AI's dictation is now capable of "automatically handling capitalization, punctuation, and formatting" as speak, though you need to enable it manually. Advanced Dictation Preview is only available to iPhones that support Siri AI's most powerful features, including the iPhone 17 Pro series and iPhone Air. You can enable it by going to Settings > General > Keyboard > Advanced Dictation Preview.

iOS 27 has a hidden macOS-like recovery mode, which allows you to diagnose and fix software problems without using a computer. Once you're running iOS 27 on your iPhone, you can access it with the following key presses:

Press Volume Down and release it.

Hold the Side Button (power button) till you see "Loading recovery options…" on the screen.

Note that recovery mode should be a last resort to fix your iPhone, and you should not try it without understanding the risks. More than one option in recovery mode directly formats your iPhone and erases all your data, so proceed with extreme caution.

iOS 27 introduces extra-large widgets, which take up almost all of the available screen space on your device. This allows you to view all of your calendar events in a single widget. (Finally.) To try this in iOS 27, hold an empty part of the Home Screen on your iPhone, and tap the paintbrush icon in the top-right corner. Search for "Calendar," and swipe right till you see the biggest widgets. At the time of writing, Calendar offers two of these extra-large widgets: "Up Next," and "List." Hit Add Widget to drop it to your Home Screen. You can also try other extra-large widgets such as Smart Stack, Music, and other apps that support this iOS 27 feature.

Find My allows you to share your location with your loved ones, but it can sometimes feel a bit invasive. To temporarily stop sharing your location, you could turn off your phone's GPS, but that affects all other apps which rely on location sharing features. iOS 27 has a more elegant solution, which allows you to temporarily stop sharing your location with others. To use it, open Find My, go to the People tab, and tap the three dots next to a contact's name. Under "My Location," select Hide Location, which will turn off location sharing for a day.

title: ‘Send help’: LA GOP leader issues desperate appeal after Dem mayor’s campaign vid shocks viewers
description: LA County GOP Chair Roxanne Hoge says Karen Bass's viral 6-to-1 matching funds video reveals how Democrats codified electoral 'shenanigans' into law.
fullText:
EXCLUSIVE: Los Angeles County GOP Chair Roxanne Hoge issued an impassioned appeal for Republicans to "send help" to Democratic-controlled California, describing what she sees as rampant corruption in the state and saying most people "can't understand the level of obsession they have with controlling our lives."

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Hoge addressed the online reaction to a recent viral video posted by Democratic Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass in which the mayor said the city government would match six times every dollar donated to her re-election campaign. While some social media users expressed shock, Hoge said she was not surprised.

"The rest of the country doesn't understand what we're living under here," she told Fox News Digital.

"The number one thing people need to understand about Los Angeles in particular and California in general is that they've codified all of their shenanigans," she explained. "What normal people consider cheating or weirdness in the electoral process? It's all in the rules [here]."

Los Angeles Proposal To Allow Noncitizens To Vote In Local Elections Sparks Online Backlash

In a recent viral social media post, Bass, Los Angeles' 72-year-old progressive mayor, said that "when you donate to our campaign, the city can match your donation 6 to 1," adding, "If you donate $5, the city turns it into $35."

Bass said that "thanks to LA's super match program, every qualified donation from Los Angeles residents is matched six to one by the city." She added that after this year's mayoral primary, in which Republican candidate Spencer Pratt garnered significant support, "we had to start over from scratch."

"So, we need you to rush in your matching donation right now, to help fuel this campaign," she said.

Social media users questioned and criticized Bass' comments.

Conservative activist Billboard Chris commented, "How is it legal to take money from Los Angeles taxpayers to fund your own re-election campaign?" Commentator Matt Van Swol wrote, "Can someone please explain to me like I'm 5 years old how this is not COMPLETELY illegal?????"

Karen Bass Ripped After Suggesting Taxpayer-funded Dental Care For Meth Users

Author Michael Shellenberger simply wrote, "This is grotesque."

"Is this a JOKE?!?" wrote well-known Los Angeles doctor and political commentator Houman David Hemmati. "Why on EARTH are LA City taxpayers, who can't even afford to clean up their streets or have water in their fire hydrants, forced to match contributions to Bass' Mayoral reelection campaign 6:1?!? … HUH?! Insanity!"

Hoge, however, said the matching-funds program Bass describes in her campaign video is legal under city law. Los Angeles voters approved a public campaign-financing system in 1990 that the City Council later expanded into today's six-to-one matching-funds program. Donations are subject to caps and eligibility rules.

"Voters passed something that sounded so good; they always sound so good at the beginning. Public financing matching funds for campaigns on a one-to-one basis. That seems great, right?" she said. "And then it transmogrifies … into what we have today, this many-headed hydra of insanity where taxpayers are on the hook for $6 for every dollar raised by a city of L.A. candidate."

She noted that the rule applies not only to mayoral campaigns but also to City Council campaigns, adding that they "Have many active [Democratic Socialists of America] members currently sitting and running."

Hoge said "the message that Karen Bass is sending is the same message that those of us who live here behind the blue curtain have been getting for decades."

"And that is, 'Forget it, Jake, it's Chinatown. Don't try to go against City Hall,'" she said.

Shocking Percentage Of Democrats Identify As 'Democratic Socialists' According To New Poll: 'Toxic Policies'

"We saw Spencer Pratt mount a very strong argument for sanity and good governance. It wasn't partisan, what he was saying. It was pure common sense, and they rose up because they were threatened."

Fox News Digital reached out to Bass' campaign and office for comment.

Despite California's political landscape, Hoge urged Republicans not to write off America's most populous state as a lost cause.

"California is totally worth fighting for because it is an absolute gem," she said, adding, "We are living with people who gleefully would reach into the shower and change the temperature while you're having a bath."

Addressing Republicans directly, she said, "We belong to the leave me alone party."

"California, being in the west, is the ultimate place where you should be free to write your own story. And that, I think, is the number one thing people have to remember," she said. "They need to send help."
